articles.title: Nations Championship - Ireland 42-12 Argentina: Hugo Keenan scores hat-trick in statement victory for Andy Farrell's charges in Dublin
articles.summary: Hugo Keenan (hat-trick), Dan Sheehan, Sam Prendergast, Ronan Kelleher score tries as Ireland secure dominant bonus-point success over Argentina in Nations Championship at Aviva Stadium in Dublin; Likes of Mack Hansen, Ryan Baird, Rob Baloucoune, Nick Timoney and Tadhg Beirne also shine
articles.body:
On a night of big positives for Andy Farrell's charges, they scored six tries through full-back Keenan's three, hooker Dan Sheehan, fly-half Sam Prendergast and replacement front row Ronan Kelleher.

Argentina scored two tries through wing Mateo Carreras, and actually landed the opener in the Test, but by 55 minutes the contest was over, with the visitors totally outplayed.

Indiscipline also proved a thorn for the Pumas again as centre Justo Piccardo and replacement lock Efraín Elias were shown costly yellow cards, with a vibrant Ireland needing little invitation to attack and score points.

A typically cagey and physical beginning to the fixture saw the visitors strike for the opening try in the 10th minute - wing Carreras claiming an inch-perfect Tomás Albornoz kick-pass over the head of final defender Craig Casey in a wonderful piece of playmaking skill.

The Irish response came within five minutes, though, as a Casey-led counter-ruck earned territory, before a scintillating backline move saw Robert Baloucoune arc round and make great yards at pace, Mack Hansen offload inside brilliantly, and Keenan collect to finish.

Prendergast added the conversion for an early lead after Albornoz had earlier failed off the tee, while three superb Irish turnovers soon earned them the chance to strike again.

First, flanker Nick Timoney exquisitely won a breakdown penalty by his own try-line to quell a Pumas surge. Then, Tadhg Beirne got up to steal an Argentina lineout, while Timoney came up with the breakdown goods again soon after - this time on the halfway line.

When Ireland kicked to touch and into 22, an intricate move off a lineout saw Sheehan play a blind inside ball for Timoney to charge forward. The Ulster flanker was stopped just short, but quick Casey service saw Sheehan fly over for a 14-5 lead.

Five minutes later, Ireland had their third try through Keenan again. Ryan Baird won another lineout steal to instigate the attack, with Ireland's full-back then doing marvellously well to battle and bounce his way over past a number of Argentina defenders.

When Prendergast converted, the Irish lead stood at 21-5, and worse looked likely to follow when Pumas centre Piccardo was sin-binned for giving away a cynical penalty in not being back 10 metres off a Sheehan quick-tap penalty.

Ireland failed to add a fourth score before the break, however, as Sheehan was illegally halted in the corner by replacement Leonel Oviedo - referee Luke Pearce just about decreeing penalty-only was sufficient.

Ireland put it behind them to score their bonus-point clinching fourth try less than two minutes into the second half, with Prendergast throwing a dummy bought by Marcos Kremer and racing in from deep.

The Pumas replied with their second try four minutes later, when centre Santiago Chocobares made the key break and Carreras powered his way over past Keenan, but Ireland then kicked on to another level.

The tireless Beirne won a trademark breakdown penalty deep in the Argentina half to earn the platform, with quick hands from Tadhg Furlong, Joe McCarthy and then Baird giving Keenan the space to dive over for his third.

With Baird continuing to cause havoc at the Argentina lineout with steals, the Pumas were soon back down to 14 players when the TMO showed images of Elias catching Keenan high in a shoulder-to-head tackle.

From the very next lineout, Ireland constructed a tight maul which drove forward at pace and was finished by Kelleher for their sixth try of the night.

Replacement Ciaran Frawley's conversion brought Ireland to their eventual 42-12 score, and head coach Farrell will be irked somewhat they failed to add more points from what was left in the Test.

Hansen showed some sensational skill and came close to both creating and scoring tries in what remained, but Kelleher's lineout performance was the central reason behind the home side failing to score more tries - the replacement coughing up a host of possession at the set-piece.

Farrell 'delighted' with win but warns: 'We have to be more ruthless'

Ireland head coach Andy Farrell said post-match:

"First and foremost, delighted to get the win and a good win at that. Six tries to two says a lot.

"Delighted to get the season off with a big win but I think the first game, we will learn a lot from that. It's a good place to be.

"We started really well in terms of being really clinical, we got into the 22 and scored two tries. We were dominant in that territory, which is what you want at this level.

"If you look at Hugo Keenan, Ryan Baird and Andrew Porter, lads who have not played international rugby in a while who have stepped up, Mack Hansen is another one, so I'm delighted for them.

"How we can be a bit more ruthless [is a lesson to take], because that's the team we want to be."

Keenan: Still a lot of work for us to do and get better at

Ireland's player of the match, Hugo Keenan said:

" You miss it. It's been 21 months since I've been here [Aviva Stadium] in green and it's been tough watching on.

"A bit like the rest of the lads, I'm just delighted to be out here and wanting to make this brilliant crowd proud and do them justice.

"I was at the end of three good plays, they were walk-ins to be honest, I'll take any.

"We got a bonus point playing against a really tough Argentina side. To beat them by 30 points and not play to our full potential is exciting because there is a lot to work on and get better at.

"We know every point counts. It's three tough games. We need to put ourselves in the best position and worry about what we can control."

"I think we were very good in patches, and some of the tries we scored were proper team tries.

"We'll be walking away from that game thinking we could have got a lot more out of it. There were some good parts for sure, but there's certainly a lot of parts we could have been better.

"It's a great starting point for us, we know we need to keep improving. Fiji will be a challenge, we know they like to throw the ball about, and South Africa after that, but all eyes on Fiji. We need to keep improving the performance."

For Ireland, they next face Fiji in their second Nations Championship Test of the autumn at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin on Saturday, November 14 (8.10pm kick-off).

Argentina travel to face Italy in Genoa for their next Test, also on Saturday November 14 (11.40am kick-off GMT).

articles.title: England rugby: Jamie George says squad 'hurt' by article that reported rift with Steve Borthwick this summer
articles.summary: Jamie George insists the England squad "are all massively behind Steve [Borthwick] in every way possible" as they prepare for Nations Championship game vs Australia on Sunday; England squad addressed media reports of issues between players and coach
articles.body:
The Times reported that some England players lost faith in Borthwick during a summer campaign with included a 45-21 defeat to world champions South Africa and a nervy win over Argentina.

It is alleged players objected to Borthwick's treatment of them, that he was involved in a training ground bust-up with Ellis Genge and that they wanted RFU chief executive Bill Sweeney - who this week unequivocally backed the head coach - to listen to their gripes.

Speaking to Sky Sports News on Friday, hooker George, captain for the July tour with Maro Itoje rested and named in the starting XV to face the Wallabies this weekend, says the squad addressed the article and will use it to "galavanise" them.

The 36-year-old, who insisted England are "all massively behind Steve in every way possible" said: "I'm really disappointed with the article that's been written. There's not a huge amount of truth to any of it, really.

"I think the timing of it is shocking, to be completely honest. Releasing it two days before a Test match is always trying to be divisive, in my opinion.

"I think that we're all quite hurt. We have made sure that we aren't distracted by it, but also allowing us to be galvanised by it, in a way, because we want to defend Steve.

"We are all massively behind Steve in every way possible. I think probably, unfortunately for them, it won't be divisive and it might be quite galvanising for us."

'We have to look after Steve in every way we know how'

George continued: "We had to address it. I spoke to [captain] Maro [Itoje] last night. I don't like elephants in rooms.

"I just think that everything is much better out in the open. And we did exactly that. Maro spoke brilliantly, opened it up. George Ford then spoke brilliantly. It's done now.

"We're upset by it. We are disappointed with it.

"At the same time, we're seeing it for what it is and understanding that we've got a really important role to step up now and look after Steve in every way that we know how.

"The best way to do that is by putting out a brilliant performance on Sunday."

Harlequins' Fin Baxter, who has only played two games since returning from 10 months out with a foot injury, will start at loosehead prop against Australia, with George lavishing praise on the 24-year-old.

George added of Baxter: "I am going to be very careful as I don't want to give too many superlatives to Fin but I honestly think he is one of the best props I have played with.

"He is physically incredible with a baby face, which I love. He is strong. But the thing about Fin I love the most is his game-feel, his understanding.

"As a loosehead prop, there aren't many in the world that are able to do it in the way he does. He is a huge asset to our team."

After facing Australia on Sunday (3.10pm kick-off), England go on to play Japan and New Zealand on November 14 and November 21 respectively, before the Nations Championship finals weekend across November 27-29.

articles.title: Scotland v New Zealand: Hosts come full circle for another crack at All Blacks
articles.summary: Sione Tuipulotu and Scotland have the chance to end one of sport's longest-standing hoodoos against New Zealand on Saturday, writes Andy Burke.
articles.body:
As Scotland prepare for their latest attempt at busting one of sport's longest standing hoodoos against the All Blacks on Saturday, it is worth reflecting on the journey this team has been on since their last tilt 12 months ago.

That match, in which Scotland fell 17-0 down, roared back to 17-17, only to succumb to the sorcery of Damien McKenzie late in the game, was another experience to file in Scottish rugby's bulging folder marked 'Ones That Got Away'.

It was a bitter disappointment, but worse was to follow when a 21-0 lead against Argentina spiralled into a nightmarish defeat that led to serious questions around the future of head coach Gregor Townsend.

The heat was turned up further still by a dispiriting loss to Italy in Rome to kick off this year's Six Nations. Since then, Scotland have flipped the narrative.

They smashed England's 12-game winning run to smithereens, delivered one of the greatest displays in the history of the national side by putting 50 points on Grand Slam-chasing France, stuck seven tries on Argentina in their own backyard in the summer then ran world champions South Africa close in an epic Test match in Pretoria.

As Jack Dempsey said recently on the BBC Scotland Rugby Podcast: "We can be the best team in the world for 20 minutes and we can be the worst team in the world for 20 minutes." The hope is the experiences of the past year will help them deliver more of the former and less of the latter.

Captain Sione Tuipulotu admitted: "We've been through a lot in the last 12 months, as a coaching staff, as a playing group and as a team.

"We've probably had to walk a path where we've had to support each other, had to pick each other up after defeats but also had some landmark victories in there as well.

"I do feel like we've progressed a lot in the last 12 months. It's been those experiences that have allowed us to progress.

"For instance, in Pretoria against the world champions. Having those type of experiences that I think as a team we haven't really been exposed to a lot previously, certainly not in the time I've been playing for Scotland."

Scotland can be best & worst team in world - Dempsey

Scotland face more ambitious All Blacks - Townsend

No end in sight for Russell as he eyes famous All Blacks win

Comparing the French side Scotland put away so impressively in March to the New Zealand team that will run out at Murrayfield, it is hard to argue this match represents a significant step up in class.

Regular exposure to France in the Six Nations - and beating them six times in the Townsend era - means they do not carry, despite their undeniable class, the sort of aura the All Blacks still retain when they rock up in Edinburgh.

That sense of missed opportunity last year came from the number of chances Scotland left behind and also the feeling that the 2025 iteration in the final months of Scott Robertson's reign was not vintage All Blacks.

Dave Rennie, the former Glasgow Warriors head coach, with ex-Scotland scrum-half Mike Blair by his side, seems to have reset the All Blacks back to their factory settings - pace, power, ambition and freedom to play. "A proper All Blacks team," as Townsend described them this week.

"They look like a group that's together," Tuipulotu said.

"You could see that in the Greatest Rivalry series [against South Africa]. I thought the way Ardie [Savea] was leading the boys before he got hurt was pretty inspirational.

"I thought that really brought them together since he's gone down [injured]. Other boys have had to step up, but I thought his mark on the All Blacks as a leader was evident.

"They've carried that on. Obviously they've had two really good victories against Australia and they're probably playing a brand that the players really enjoy.

"It's a brand of rugby that you would traditionally associate with New Zealand teams, one which the fans really enjoy.

And Tuipulotu is clear in his assessment of how Saturday's Test will go.

"A big part of this match will come down to who can be tougher for longer," he added.

Podcast: Can Scotland end 121 years of history against All Blacks?

articles.title: England v Australia: Player-coach rift report will only galvanise us - George
articles.summary: England hooker Jamie George says the squad are "really upset" by a newspaper article claiming the end of their summer tour was marked by player unrest over Steve Borthwick's leadership.
articles.body:
England hooker Jamie George says the squad are "really upset" by a newspaper article claiming the end of their summer tour was marked by player unrest over head coach Steve Borthwick's leadership.

A report in the Times , external says unhappy players wanted summit talks with Borthwick and Rugby Football Union chief executive Bill Sweeney in Argentina in July.

It alleges there are disagreements among Borthwick's wider coaching group, which has been subject to frequent change in his nearly four years in charge, and concerns over the head coach's man-management skills.

England meet Australia in the Nations Championship on Sunday at Allianz Stadium in Twickenham, with George querying the timing of the article as well as its contents.

The Saracens hooker, who was made England captain by Borthwick in 2024 before the role passed to Maro Itoje 12 months later, said that he did not recognise the situation described by the article.

"I can tell you that a lot of it's untrue," George told Rugby Union Weekly.

"We, as a squad, are incredibly disappointed by it.

"You just have to look at the timing of the article - two days out from our first Test match. I think it's clearly there to try and be divisive.

"It is the first time I think in my England career that as a group we've had to address an article that's been written, but we spoke about it brilliantly.

"Maro called a leader's meeting and thought that that was the best way of us going about it.

"Whoever's written this article, obviously their aim was for it to be divisive. Unfortunately for them, it's going to go the other way.

"This is going to galvanise us, it's going to make us tighter. We speak a lot about standing up for people, we speak a lot about helping each other, and we've got to make sure that we do that for Steve.

"He has had a bit of a personal attack here and an unwarranted one at that."

While none of the sources for the Times article were directly quoted in it, some of those previously involved in Borthwick's regime have criticised the set-up.

England's most-capped men's player Ben Youngs, who won the Premiership under Borthwick at Leicester and was part of his England squad at the 2023 Rugby World Cup, has described how he felt the head coach failed to offer sympathy and support when his family was affected by a terminal illness. , external

Defence coach Felix Jones helped South Africa to back-to-back world titles, but lasted only seven months working under Borthwick before an "unstable working environment" reportedly motivated him to hand in his notice.

"The depiction is not something I recognise," Borthwick told Rugby Union Weekly of the Times article, emphasising that meetings between senior players and coaches are a feature of most coaching set-ups.

"As senior players part of our job is to challenge Steve," added George. "Steve is so open to us giving feedback and having challenge.

"It is very much a two-way conversation and that was definitely there in Argentina.

"There was an edge to what we were doing - there was plenty going on - but at no stage was it toxic.

"I don't know many organisations in the world that don't review big tournaments and try and make sure you take plenty of learnings."

Live commentary on BBC Sports Extra, BBC Sport website and app

England's autumn campaign begins against Australia on Sunday.

Borthwick will be acutely aware that it was at the same point in the World Cup cycle that his predecessor Eddie Jones was sacked.

The Australian, who, like Borthwick, had been heavily backed by the RFU, was eventually forced out after a November 2022 defeat by South Africa was met by a chorus of jeers from the Twickenham stands.

Allianz Stadium generates about 90% of the RFU's revenue, the vast majority of which comes via men's national team matchdays.

England's meeting with the Wallabies will be the first time Borthwick's team have returned to the venue since February's 42-21 loss to Ireland in a miserable Six Nations campaign.

While wins over Fiji and Argentina in their last two outings have ended a run of five straight losses, England's winning percentage for 2026 is still only 38%.

Only two years since the start of the Millennium have ended with a worse return.

After taking over from Jones, Borthwick very nearly led England to the Rugby World Cup final less than a year later, losing to South Africa by a single point in their semi-final.

His 2025 campaign fuelled hope with 11 wins from 12 matches, including a rare victory over New Zealand.

However, the momentum gathered on that run has evaporated.

The All Blacks, rejuvenated under new coach Dave Rennie, loom two weeks after Sunday's meeting with Australia, with a match against Japan, now led by Jones himself, in between.

articles.title: Ireland 42-12 Argentina: Hugo Keenan scores hat-trick as six-try hosts punish Pumas
articles.summary: Hugo Keenan scores a hat-trick of tries as Ireland open the home leg of the Nations Championship with a commanding bonus-point win over Argentina in Dublin.
articles.body:
Tries: Keenan 3, Sheehan, Prendergast, Kelleher Cons: Prendergast 5, Frawley

Hugo Keenan scored a hat-trick of tries as Ireland opened the home leg of the Nations Championship with a commanding bonus-point win over Argentina in Dublin.

In addition to Keenan, captain Dan Sheehan, Sam Prendergast and Ronan Kelleher crossed as Andy Farrell's side punished a messy and ill-disciplined Pumas outfit, who scored twice through wing Mateo Carreras.

On a deeply disappointing night for Argentina, who are still without an away win over Ireland after 12 attempts, Justo Piccardo and Ephraim Elias were sin-binned while they lost captain Julian Montoya to a failed head injury assessment before half-time.

But having closed the summer with a 40-21 loss to New Zealand in Auckland, it was a satisfying evening for Ireland, who move top of the northern hemisphere table before France, Scotland and England's matches this weekend.

With an opening home win secured, Ireland host Fiji next week before world champions South Africa visit Dublin on 21 November, while Argentina travel to Italy and France after a third defeat in four games.

Keenan, Baird and Beirne reflect on win over Argentina

Reaction and recap as Ireland comfortably beat Pumas

Fixtures and standings as Nations Championship returns

In 2024 and 2025, Ireland opened the autumn with dispiriting defeats by the All Blacks, but Argentina were not able to offer a similarly unforgiving examination here.

But the Pumas, who arrived in Dublin with just one win in six this year, initially silenced the crowd with a beautifully worked try.

Following a patient multi-phase attack, out-half Tomas Albornoz booted to the corner, where Carreras towered above diminutive Ireland scrum-half Craig Casey to claim the ball and score.

Casey was one of the surprise Irish selections, having been picked ahead of long-time Farrell favourite Jamison Gibson-Park. To his credit, Casey shook off his mismatch with Carreras to win the turnover penalty that put Ireland on the front foot for the first time as Argentina quickly lost their early momentum.

From the resulting line-out, Ireland's back three collectively carved Argentina open. The excellent Rob Baloucoune tore through midfield and offloaded to Hansen, who defied pressure from Bautista Delguy to send Keenan through.

Similar to Casey's selection, the inclusion of Nick Timoney ahead of Josh van der Flier was reflective of Farrell's intent to shake things up.

A thoroughly dependable operator, Timoney impressed at open-side flanker in the first half, turning Albornoz over before popping up in a line-out strike play to put Sheehan through for Ireland's second.

With the Argentine set-piece already creaking, the returning Ryan Baird stole a line-out and set Ireland on their way to a third as Hansen found Keenan again for the British and Irish Lions full-back's second.

Already trailing 21-5, Argentina's resolve was severely tested in the closing minutes of the half.

Having lost outside centre Piccardo to a yellow card, captain Montoya failed a head injury assessment (HIA), but when his replacement Leonel Oviedo was also went withdrawn for a HIA, loose-head prop Boris Wenger was forced to fill in at hooker.

Ireland also lost Sheehan to a head knock after he was denied a second try.

Within two minutes of the restart, Prendergast - who shook off a wrist injury to start at fly-half - darted through a hole in the Argentina defence to score his first international try and secure the bonus point.

While Carreras pounced for his second three minutes later following an enterprising run from Santiago Chocobares, Keenan completed his hat-trick following a clever offload from Baird, taking the 30-year-old's Nations Championship tally to five after scores against Australia and New Zealand.

As fatigue set in for Argentina, Kelleher touched down following a maul with a try that further sucked the energy out of the game following Elias' yellow card for a high hit on Keenan.

With the game beyond Argentina, both sides were guilty of messy passages as the game wore on, with Ireland replacement tight-head prop Sam Illo yellow carded on the hour for driving early at a maul.

While a seventh try eluded the Irish, Farrell will likely be contented rather than thrilled by his side's performance, with slick passages and fine finishing mixed with the odd careless moment.

However, while Argentina were a shadow of the adventurous attacking unit that pushed Ireland all the way in 2024 and beat Farrell's British and Irish Lions in Dublin last year, a 30-point win is a solid platform from which the Irish can build as they switch focus to Fiji before another mouthwatering tussle with the Springboks.

articles.title: Prem Rugby Cup: Wins for Northampton Saints and Sale Sharks
articles.summary: Northampton keep their hopes of reaching the Prem Rugby Cup semi-finals alive with a dominant derby win over Leicester.
articles.body:
Northampton kept their hopes of reaching the Prem Rugby Cup semi-finals alive after a dominant 39-19 derby victory over East Midlands rivals Leicester.

A youthful Saints line-up turned on the style to sink the holders at Franklin's Gardens and stretch Northampton's run to 16 successive home wins in all competitions.

Wings Tom Rowe and Amena Caqusau and full-back James Martin all touched down twice in a seven-try romp for the Saints.

After three successive defeats in the Prem Rugby Cup, last season's winners Leicester are bottom of Pool B.

It was not a perfect evening for Northampton. Already without two injured scrum-halves in England international Alex Mitchell and Archie McParland, the Saints lost a third in the 29th minute in Jonny Weimann.

The 20-year-old, made captain for the evening, limped off after creating Northampton's first two tries, number one in the 11th minute with a glorious long pass to Martin and number two five minutes later with a cross-kick to Rowe.

But England Under-18s scrum-half Sonny Goode showed Northampton's remarkable depth in the position with an impressive showing off the bench.

After being steamrollered in a feisty Prem meeting at Mattioli Woods Welford Road a fortnight ago, this emphatic win provided a measure of revenge.

Saints led 27-7 at the break with Rowe, Caqusau and centre Toby Thame also crossing.

Caqusau produced a fine finish to secure the bonus point for Saints in the 36th minute and Rowe's second on the stroke of half-time gave Saints their 20-point interval advantage.

But Martin went over for his second from a cross-kick in the 46th minute and then Caqusau added his second after some fine approach play by Goode with Leicester wing Adam Radwan in the sin-bin.

Leicester, well beaten, managed three tries, two from hooker Sam Moli and one from back row Osian Thomas.

Sale Sharks went to the top of Pool A with a tense 21-19 win over Bristol Bears at the CorpAcq Stadium.

Two tries from Arron Reed - playing at full-back - and one from Alex Wills did the damage but Bristol took the game to the wire with two tries from Max Pepper after Totoa Auvaa, the Samoan hooker given a second chance by director of rugby Pat Lam following his sacking by Saracens for his off-field conduct, had opened their account.

Sam Worsley had a chance to win it for the Bears four minutes from time but was short with a long-range penalty attempt.

articles.title: Ireland 42-12 Argentina: Six tries and a big win - but were Andy Farrell's side ruthless?
articles.summary: Despite a six-try and 30-point win over Argentina, Andy Farrell and Tadhg Beirne admit Ireland could have been more ruthless in Friday's win.
articles.body:
Before Ireland's Nations Championship game with Argentina, head coach Andy Farrell had been honest about where his side are less than a year out from the World Cup.

He admitted his team must improve if they are to challenge in Australia next year - a stark contrast to four years ago when they were riding the crest of a wave before they fell short in the quarter-finals.

Despite Mateo Carreras' early try, Ireland had far too much for Los Pumas in Dublin as they ran out 42-12 winners under the Friday night lights.

Hugo Keenan stole the headlines with his hat-trick, while Dan Sheehan, Sam Prendergast and Ronan Kelleher also crossed.

But despite scoring six tries and winning by a 30-point margin, Farrell was left wanting more.

Ireland had 59% territory throughout the game, and also edged possession, but did not score after the 55th minute when Kelleher rounded off a rolling maul.

"The scoreline is a good one because not many teams do that to Argentina, they are a dangerous side," Farrell said.

"I thought there was outstanding stuff and some clinical stuff, but I think the story of the game is we missed a chance to be ruthless.

"Having said that, the opportunities we had in the right end of the field showed the dominance in field position and territory."

Keenan hat-trick as six-try Ireland beat Pumas

Keenan, Baird and Beirne reflect on win over Argentina

One concern for Farrell will be an injury list - and a lengthy one at that.

Captain Sheehan was forced off in the first half after he failed a head injury assessment, although Farrell said he "seems fine in the dressing room".

Wing Robert Baloucoune also went off with a knock, while Sean Jansen sustained a "bang" to his knee and Josh van der Flier and Mack Hansen both have ankle concerns.

The injuries to Baloucoune, who departed in the 58th minute, and Hansen, who continued after receiving treatment, will be particularly concerning after the performance of Farrell's back three.

They had only played once together before, four years ago against South Africa, and Keenan's first try of the evening came off the back of a flowing move, when Baloucoune powered into space and found Hansen, who in turn set up the full-back to score.

That was the catalyst for Ireland's turnaround - and a hat-trick for Keenan in his first home match since the 2025 Six Nations came a year since Hansen's treble against Australia in Dublin.

All of Farrell's back three trio have struggled with injuries in the past year, and Friday's win was a glimpse of Ireland's attacking potential if they can stay fit and in form.

"I thought the back three were outstanding. Hugo Keenan, 22 months since he played here and didn't remember what side of the pitch we warmed up, which was a bit of an insult.

"He was immense. Same with Mack and Rob. They pace they put onto the ball and they were a threat. I'm delighted with the back three."

Beirne said that Argentina "came out firing" in Dublin as they chased a first away win over Ireland, something that came as no surprise to the Irish pack.

"We weathered the storm and got into how we wanted to play the game," said Beirne.

"What was pleasing about that was some of those tries were proper team tries and everyone was involved with them. That was the biggest takeaway from the game that."

But, like Farrell, the second row believes there is more to come at the attacking end of the pitch.

"We probably came away a little bit frustrated because we felt we didn't capitalise on a lot of the territory at the end of the game and the chances we had.

"That shows how good a performance it was to come away feeling like that."

After a bruising opener, Farrell will be forced to assess his squad ahead of Fiji's visit to Dublin on 14 November.

After that, world champions South Africa will be a stern test before the finals weekend in London to round out the international window.

He had offered Craig Casey a chance to impress at scrum-half as first-choice Jamison Gibson-Park returns to full fitness, and he impressed after a slow start.

Ulster back row Nick Timoney also put in a big performance, while Prendergast's showing at fly-half was also largely positive as he put his stamp on the 10 jersey.

When asked if the performances gave him food for thought for selections for the rest of the window, Farrell said: "Definitely, 100%.

"That's exactly what you are after going into next week.

"Having some good competition, we've had it for 10 days in training so how they performed highlights how they have been training.

"Whatever side we pick next week, they'll be competing to play the following week."

articles.title: Wales v Japan: Nations Championship date starts pivotal month for Welsh rugby
articles.summary: With a World Cup on the horizon and plenty of uncertainty remaining, Steve Tandy's side hope to give the game in Wales a boost.
articles.body:
Welsh rugby's autumn series always seems to creep up on you.

It provides the first glimpse of winter and Welsh rugby fans will be hoping there is not much more discontent over the next four weeks.

There is a new tournament to be embraced as the inaugural Nations Championship returns with three rounds of games to follow the opening trio of matches in July.

With a win and two defeats in the first half of the tournament, Wales host Japan on Saturday before further games against New Zealand and Australia in Cardiff.

The 12 sides will then descend on the Allianz Stadium in Twickenham for a fourth set of matches with a three-day finals weekend to determine final placings.

November could prove a pivotal month for Welsh rugby, in more ways than one.

How will Wales fare on Nations Championship return?

First up for Wales is the now familiar foe of Eddie Jones' Japan - the teams will be facing each other for a fourth time in 16 months.

There is also the distinct possibility that the two sides could be paired together again at Twickenham at the end of the month in the tournament finale.

Wales have won two out of those three games against Japan since July 2025, with the last-gasp win in Cardiff a year ago giving head coach Steve Tandy his first Test victory.

Tandy is now preparing for his fourth campaign and has two further tournaments ahead before leading Wales into the World Cup in Australia in just under a year.

He has won three games and suffered nine defeats in 12 internationals, with another victory in the uncapped international against Barbarians.

Wales stand 10th in the world rankings with that hat-trick of Test victories coming against Fiji (ranked ninth), Italy (11th) and Japan (12th).

"We're probably on par with where I'd like us to be but we want to kick on faster than we have done,” said Tandy.

"If you look at where we were 12 months ago, the boys had won just one of 26 matches. Now we've started winning again, with four victories in 13 matches."

The Wales head coach refused to give a target of how many games his side ought to win this autumn. The Welsh public, however, should expect two victories, to show some progress and at least push a top-eight nation like Australia close.

Tandy does, though, insist that where Wales finish in the inaugural Nations Championship is important.

"It always matters, we want to finish as high up in any tournament but the only thing we can control is our performance," he said.

"We understand we're going to have to hit the ground running quickly."

Captain Dewi Lake backed this up by saying Wales are in the best state he can remember heading into a campaign.

Will English-based players shine for Wales?

There can be no excuses against Japan, who are down to a third-choice fly-half and number eight, despite the tourists these days boasting a monster forward pack.

A home defeat, and Wales face a failed autumn campaign after just one weekend of action.

Tandy also has a number of in-form players at his disposal. One of the week's narratives has been how well Welsh players are performing in the English Prem.

It is underlined by Tandy picking a record 12 players from English clubs in his 23, with nine - including six forwards - in his first XV.

Starters such as Nicky Smith, Jac Morgan, Aaron Wainwright and Dewi Lake have outlined how their games have improved since joining English clubs.

A steady selection policy will also be important with Tandy having just named a sixth centre partnership in 13 internationals by partnering Max Llewellyn with Eddie James.

"We'll have to have an open mind because there are four pretty big Test matches, back-to-back," said Tandy.

"There will naturally be changes, whether it be rotation or because of injuries, but also we've got players in certain positions we feel could be brought in."

Players picked on form not club location - Tandy

Morgan aims to show new attacking threat for Wales

Wales players in Prem doing nation proud - Smith

While eyes will be on the team and their performance on the pitch, they will also be fixated on how many empty seats will be in the Principality Stadium stands.

Unwanted records have already been set during the past 12 months. The 50,185 that watched the opening game against Argentina in 2025's autumn series was the lowest for a non-Covid era game since 2016.

Three months later, 57,744 for the 54-12 hammering by France in February was the smallest Six Nations crowd seen in Cardiff.

Some readily comparative targets this month will be the 61,324 and 68,388 that were given as attendances for games against Japan and New Zealand a year ago.

Welsh rugby is fascinated with crowd numbers but there is an important financial element to them.

The Welsh Rugby Union (WRU) relies on attendances at men's international matches for more than half its turnover.

So, empty seats would represent badly needed lost revenue with the WRU having announced an £18m loss last month.

Wales players, including the popular and well-connected Louis Rees-Zammit, have been on their social media accounts posting ticket links.

Lake hopes the squad's performances can bring back the fans.

"We've built massive connections with supporters over the last 18 months in terms of on-field stuff," said the hooker.

"They can see the passion and care we show when representing them, the jersey and the country.

"We know it's on us to excite them and to make them bring noise. It's not just going to happen on its own."

Murchie demands major improvement in Wales defence

Jones looks to create Japan history in Cardiff

Jones - the smiling wind-up artist who refuses to fade away

Filling the ground is not just the squad's responsibility. The WRU also has to look at themselves.

Reasons for fans saying they are staying away will include the cost of tickets and the day out itself, although there have been a number of concessions this autumn.

There are also the previous results of the men's side and the continued apathy towards the Welsh rugby soap opera which shows no sign of abating.

Before this season started, you had Wales captain Lake citing one of his reasons for leaving Ospreys for Gloucester was the uncertainty surrounding the Welsh game, and expressing his relief that he would not have to deal with that issue on a daily basis.

That should prove a wake-up call. The Wales men's senior team could deflect from those concerns by winning games in the next year - but the underlying issues remain.

Public faith and confidence in the WRU is very low because of the manner in which the game has been governed in the past, and how it is being handled currently.

On the one hand, the WRU board are determined to cut a professional side by 2028.

The governing body has announced they will award licences to Cardiff and Dragons. That pits Ospreys and Scarlets against each other for the west Wales licence with a final decision expected by the summer of 2027.

Then you have the new WRU chair Lyndon Faulkner coming in and suggesting he will look at everything, including keeping four professional sides.

You also have the latest twist of the WRU trying to get two sides into an Anglo-Welsh tournament, the same number of professional teams the Union initially wanted when they first announced their reduction policy.

Confused? You would not be alone. Is it two, three or four teams? What league will they play in? Has the plan changed again?

The futures of players and coaches are at stake. Supporters want to know whether their team will continue to exist.

Ironically, securing an Anglo-Welsh league and leaving the United Rugby Championship (URC) would probably improve the WRU’s popularity among sections of the Welsh public.

There will be an annual general meeting (AGM) the day after Wales play Australia this month, and a rugby summit has been proposed for December, where supporters will hope clarity and transparency is provided.

Before then, Wales have four rugby games to try and win, starting today. An opening victory will ensure Welsh rugby starts the month in a brighter place.

RFU boss confirms WRU Anglo-Welsh league approach

articles.title: Rugby League World Cup 2026: New Zealand sweep Samoa aside to reach Women's World Cup final
articles.summary: New Zealand's women will hope it is fourth time lucky after defeating Samoa 32-0 to reach next Sunday's Rugby League World Cup final.
articles.body:
Tries: Wiki, Waaka 3, Hufanga, Atai, McGregor Goals: Kiria-Ratu 2

New Zealand's women will hope it is fourth time lucky after defeating Samoa 32-0 to reach next Sunday's Rugby League World Cup final.

It will be the Kiwi Ferns' seventh successive appearance in the showpiece match, but having won the first three between 2000-2008, three trips to the final since then have all ended in heartache.

Three consecutive losses to Australia included a blowout 54-4 scoreline four years ago at Old Trafford and unless debutants Fiji spring one of the greatest upsets in the tournament's history in the other semi-final, the Jillaroos are likely to again provide the substantial obstacle to New Zealand becoming four-time champions.

However, on Saturday, New Zealand made light of the blustery and difficult conditions inside Newcastle's McDonald Jones Stadium, in New South Wales, to make their case as potential winners.

Mackenzie Wiki's try - less than two minutes into proceedings, off the back of a Samoa error - set the tone for the Kiwi Ferns.

As the storm clouds began to gather overhead, New Zealand's dual-code international Stacey Waaka capitalised on some indecision from Samoa winger Mercedez Taulelei-Siala to collect and ground Raecene McGregor's kick.

It was efficient and highly professional from New Zealand, who conceded just 24 points across their three group games and once again exhibited their defensive parsimony during a hard-fought first period.

A combination of that and Samoa's inability to make the most of field position, with a smattering of handling errors thrown in as well, laid the platform for New Zealand's triumph.

There were notable bright spots for the Samoa fans to enjoy.

Fanua Rimoni was a powerful and dominant presence at lock forward, while teenage winger Anastasia Leatupue produced a nerveless showing on her international bow.

Samoa's biggest disappointment was that they could not get the ball into the hands of the 18-year-old in good attacking positions - with Pauline Piliae-Rasabale twice pulled up for forward passes on the right edge in an error-strewn display.

But just like in the first 35 minutes, they had no answer to New Zealand's more potent attacking threat.

Waaka was again the beneficiary of a pinpoint McGregor kick as she crossed for her second try and Mele Hufanga held off the attentions of three Samoa defenders tfor her score.

It was a feat that was matched by Kaiyah Atai just over two minutes later as New Zealand went through the gears.

With Samoa's resistance gradually waning, Waaka capped a fine individual display with her hat-trick and McGregor scored the try her performance richly deserved to round off a fine New Zealand display.

Waaka scores hat-trick as New Zealand reach Women's RL World Cup final - as it happened

Matt's player of the match: Stacey Waaka

It takes a big performance to steal the limelight away from the blockbusting Mele Hufanga in the Kiwis back-line but cross-code star Stacey Waaka did just that with an impressive display.

She cut Samoa open with searing breaks, cranking out 131 metres, and ran in a hat-trick - including a perfectly timed run to collect Raecene McGregor's deft kick - added to two line breaks and line break assists, a try assist and three tackle breaks.

New Zealand took their time to get going, and Waaka's influence was key to making that step.

Image caption, Stacey Waaka is playing at her first Rugby League World Cup

articles.title: Nations Championship - Scotland 21-43 New Zealand: All Blacks power on to leave hosts well short of history at Murrayfield
articles.summary: Wallace Sititi, Ethan de Groot, Codie Taylor, Beauden Barrett (two), Josh Moorby, Asafo Aumua score as New Zealand's All Blacks surge on in second half to comprehensively beat Scotland at Murrayfield in Nations Championship; Scots fail to score four tries, meaning they earn no bonus point
articles.body:
The All Blacks scored seven tries in the Scottish capital through No 8 Wallace Sititi, loosehead Ethan de Groot, hooker Codie Taylor, full-back Beauden Barrett (two), wing Josh Moorby and replacement hooker Asafo Aumua, and despite sin-binings to back-rows Peter Lakai and Sititi, demonstrated their lethal ability in attack.

Scotland battled from 10 points behind to narrow to within three by the break after a madcap opening 40 minutes which saw hooker Ewan Ashman score a hat-trick, but New Zealand emerged to dominate the second half.

The net result means Gregor Townsend's side remain searching for a first success over the All Blacks, with Scotland's winless run against New Zealand now at 34 Tests.

With Scotland caught offside less than three minutes in, New Zealand turned down a potential kick for points in favour of a lineout attack in the 22, and struck for the opening try through a clever set-piece play filled with disguise as Sititi spun and raced over.

McKenzie poorly missed the conversion and within four minutes, Scotland had their first try: a rolling maul seeing the hosts plunge the majority of their outfield players in, rendering it unstoppable, with Ashman finishing.

Russell converted for an early lead, but the All Blacks replied with two bouts of sustained phase-attack in the Scotland 22: the first seeing Will Jordan held up, but the second bringing a try for De Groot as the prop grounded on the line.

McKenzie converted this time for a 12-7 lead, and it was soon extended further when Scotland No 8 Jack Dempsey gave away an extremely costly neck-roll penalty within his own 22 - the All Blacks making him pay with a rapid maul drive off a flat and sharp Taylor lineout delivery - the hooker adding the scoring touch.

McKenzie proved off target again with the conversion to leave the difference a 10-point one, and when the visitors conceded five penalties in quick succession to invite Scottish pressure in their 22, Lakai was sent to the sin-bin and Russell kicked back into the corner.

Incisive Scotland centre Huw Jones - outstanding in the first half - was held up in-goal when a try looked a certainty, but Scotland did notch their second in the 26th minute when Ashman ran a superb line to charge past Sititi to finish.

Russell tapped over the extras to narrow within three points, but the 14-player All Blacks were next to cross when Barrett sliced through following a trademark slick attack.

Scotland's response was to make another line-break off a restart, with the All Blacks guilty of yet more penalties and temporarily reduced to 13 with Sititi sin-binned.

Yet, in the home side's only attack facing 13 players, they saw a five-metre lineout maul sacked and the ball forced unplayable in a huge lost opportunity, which was then compounded when the All Blacks won a dominant scrum penalty to clear.

Another Jones break saw New Zealand infringe to present a five-metre lineout chance once more, and this time Scotland got it right two minutes before the break as backs piled into the maul again and Ashman completed his hat-trick.

Russell's conversion brought Scotland within three again by the half-time break, and an early chance fell their way in the second half on the cusp of the New Zealand 22 with ball in hand, but poor execution saw the ball fall to floor.

Instead, Scotland captain Tuipulotu was caught offside to invite New Zealand onto the attack, pinning the hosts into their 22. When a crooked lineout throw followed, New Zealand turned the screw at the scrum and scored out wide through Moorby.

The All Blacks quickly built into the 22 moments later, with Tuipulotu sin-binned for repeat team infringements and Barrett finishing his second in the 51st minute after ruthless New Zealand backline attack vs 14.

McKenzie converted for a substantial 15-point lead, which felt even greater when Scotland passed up their next try chance: wing Kyle Steyn knocking on after Jordan failed to get a hand to a long pass just in front of him.

Russell was subbed off for Scotland just past the hour having struggled to influence things, while breakdown penalties won by Jordie Barrett and Quinn Tupaea sniffed out the home side's next two possessions.

With 12 minutes to play, New Zealand chalked up their seventh try of the Test as Aumua sprinted through untouched past poor Scotland defence.

Searching for a fourth try which would at least have brought Scotland a bonus point in defeat, New Zealand's closing defence proved too good, leaving those in blue with a familiar deflating feeling.

For Scotland, they next face Australia in their second Nations Championship Test of the autumn at Murrayfield on Sunday November 15 (3.10pm kick-off).

New Zealand travel to face Wales in Cardiff for their next Test, on Saturday November 14 (2.10pm kick-off).

articles.title: Ireland Rugby Social: Ireland 'going from strength to strength' - Conor Murray
articles.summary: Former Ireland scrum-half Conor Murray says on the Ireland Rugby Social that he is impressed with how the Irish squad is progressing and their strength in depth.
articles.body:
Ireland began their autumn series of Nations Championship matches by scoring six tries in a comprehensive 42-12 win over Argentina at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin on Friday night.

Afterwards on the Ireland Rugby Social podcast, BBC Sport NI's Gavin Andrews spoke to Ireland second row Joe McCarthy about his thoughts on the game and then chatted to co-presenter and former Ireland scrum-half Conor Murray to break down the analysis of the home side's performance.

With matches against Fiji and South Africa to follow over the next couple of weeks, there was much to dissect after the win over the Pumas and assess what may be to come for the remainder of November.

You can watch the podcast now on BBC NI YouTube , external or listen on BBC Sounds.

Here are a few highlights of what Murray had to say after Ireland made it three wins from four fixtures in the competition.

On Hugo Keenan, who scored a hat-trick of tries: "Hugo stood out but he's always going to do that. He talks so much on the pitch and makes it way easier for the players around him.

"He's always marshalling the wingers and that kind of back-field system. That's Hugo in a nutshell. He's the ultimate team player.

"He looked incredibly fit, incredibly quick, explosive. He looked back to his best."

On fledgling half-back partnership Sam Prendergast and Craig Casey: "Craig and Sam marshalled the game really well. Not that there were question marks but they were a relatively new combination and it was their first time getting a big Test start together.

"Sam can forget what he's been through, I suppose the rocky start to his international career and the public scrutiny on him.

"He looks like a player who has just soaked it all in and is using it as a weapon now. He looked really sharp. He looks like he has bulked up, which is great to see too.

"There'll be a target on his back, there was already but there definitely will be now as he is such a big influence.

"We know what Craig Casey can do in terms of quick ball and magical moments but now in terms of the control of the game.

"His passing was on the money and his kicking is top notch. The overall control is probably the test that Andy Farrell gave him. He knows what he can do in loose play but in terms of controlling a Test game I thought the half-backs were brilliant."

On an impressive performance by the forwards: "[Tadhg] Furlong went really well, he's always a standard-bearer anyhow and you get top-notch performances from him, but [Andrew] Porter, another player who came back from an extended period out with injury, he's come back and showed what he's about.

"His explosiveness in open play and his fitness, he's like another back row on the field.

"Dan Sheehan, Tadhg Beirne, Joe McCarthy, Ryan Baird, the back row, across the board, all really good. I think Nick Timoney and Josh [van der Flier] are in a real battle as regards that number seven jersey."

Six tries and a big win - but were Ireland ruthless?

Keenan, Baird and Beirne reflect on win over Argentina

On strength in depth: "The depth we have now is really impressive. Over a year ago there were a good few injuries and people were worrying, not that there was panic, but wondering, 'where's the depth?' Not that we had no depth, but Andy had to blood a few players quickly.

"Those players are now in the squad and they are pushing lads across the board, pushing the other boys to perform.

"I think Irish rugby is going from strength to strength and it's really impressive to see."

On facing Fiji next week and then South Africa: "They [Ireland] should beat Fiji. I don't think that's getting ahead of ourselves. I think that's where Ireland rugby is at now.

"The lads coming in next week will be thinking they have a chance to perform and will want to be in Andy and the coaches' minds for selection for the South Africa game.

"That's how competitive the squad is. It's a real difference now that the guys coming out against Fiji aren't just saying, 'I'm getting a run out here', but rather, 'I'm actually in the mix here', which is really healthy.

"Lads deserve a chance but Andy will expect the same level of performance. When there are changes, there can be a dip because the combinations change but it's a big week of prep now and those guys will sniff an opportunity that they can stay involved.

"They won't say it but everyone wants to be involved against South Africa.

"There'll still be a core to the team that will be really, really strong, because you respect Fiji and you want some sort of consistency and some sort of momentum."

articles.title: Kalyn Ponga: New Zealand reap rewards of gamble on 'freak of nature' at Rugby League World Cup
articles.summary: Kalyn Ponga's return to Rugby League World Cup action, just 23 days after breaking his arm, was a risk. But New Zealand head coach Stacey Jones felt it was a risk worth taking - and was proved right.
articles.body:
"He's a tough character and he was so adamant he was playing."

Kalyn Ponga, in the words of his head coach Stacey Jones, was never going to miss New Zealand's Rugby League World Cup semi-final.

But it was a remarkable return to action for a player whose tournament turned from dream to nightmare just over three weeks ago.

In the World Cup opener against Australia in Sydney on 15 October, Ponga seemed to be enjoying a perfect New Zealand debut. Then it all went wrong.

The 28-year-old scored two second-half tries but was forced off late in the game - having played for 20 minutes with a broken left forearm sustained in a tackle with Cameron Munster. The Kiwis went on to lose 24-22; Ponga required surgery.

Just 23 days later, their talismanic full-back – initially named as a reserve, and then on the interchange bench – made a shock return to the starting 13 and delivered a starring performance as New Zealand overpowered Tonga 34-10 to reach their first Men's Rugby League World Cup final for 13 years.

"Where sports science is these days – I saw what he had in his arm, the rod or plate was covering his whole arm," Jones said.

"We didn't know until after our second-to-last training that he was going to be all right – he ticked all the boxes. Just a tough person."

Ponga-inspired New Zealand reach World Cup final

New Zealand sweep aside Samoa to reach Women's World Cup final

Playing with black protective bandaging taped to his left forearm, Ponga was directly involved in four of New Zealand's six tries. His fancy footwork and slick handling setting up scores for Briton Nikora, Casey McLean and Xavier Willison.

He largely dominated the contest with opposite number Lehi Hopoate, notably clearing out the full-back as he fumbled a grubber kick in Tonga's in-goal area for New Zealand's second try, scored by Dane Gagai.

In defence, a bruising try-saving block on Demitric Vaimauga indicated no cause for concern about his wounded wing.

"Obviously a freak of a player," said Kiwis captain James Fisher-Harris. "The defensive mindset he had tonight, he saved a couple of tries. That's what I love about KP.

"He's a freak of nature. His leadership skills are underrated. He's really good for us, our spine especially."

But while it was undoubtedly the Ponga show at the home of his NRL side Newcastle Knights, New Zealand are not just a one-man band.

Gagai sparked the counter-attack for McLean's try by forcing a knock-on around halfway. Jahrome Hughes added directness with his carries and when putting boot to ball. Dead-eye kicker Jamayne Isaako mastered fierce winds to kick five out of six conversions, curling two over from the left touchline, to take his tally for the tournament to 36 from 38 attempts.

Asked if this was New Zealand's best shot at adding a second title to their 2008 triumph, Fisher-Harris paused before replying: "Yes."

"We're just trying to chase history," he added. "We've only done it once but we've been building with this squad, this generation, for the past six or seven years."

'Missed opportunity' but Tonga not blaming weather

For 48 minutes, New Zealand and Tonga played with the intensity and fever of two sides seemingly locked on course for the drama of a golden-point extra-time finish.

Then the Kiwis' relentless pressure told, with two tries in five minutes extending their lead to 14 points and turning a contest into a procession.

The weather in Newcastle impacted the match from kick-off but deteriorated dramatically in the second half, with Tonga toiling in the face of howling wind and rain – conditions best encapsulated by a restart blowing back into their own half.

But head coach Kristian Woolf did not use this an excuse for his side's defeat by New Zealand, stating his team "didn't handle the conditions as well as they did".

Unbeaten through the group stage, Tonga lacked direction in attack, were guilty of poor decision-making at the end of sets, and looked vulnerable defending a bouncing ball.

"It was a disappointing way to finish. Whoever was against the wind in the second half was going to find it tough and we just had to handle it better," said Woolf.

"It's a bit of a missed opportunity with what the group's been able to do, how talented the group is, some of the footy we've played, but we just couldn't get it done tonight."

Putting the result into perspective, with Tonga playing in the semi-finals for just the second time, Woolf added: "Once upon a time, we were just happy to be in the finals and be competitive. Now, we see ourselves as real players and believe we can win it.

"We thought we could do that tonight. We certainly think we've got a team that is capable of doing that. Tongan rugby league can be really confident going forward."

The last time New Zealand had teams in both the men's and women's finals on Australian soil, they walked away with two trophies.

The year was 2008. For the men, it was a maiden title; for the women, a third consecutive crown. Neither side has lifted the trophy since then, losing a combined four finals. In Brisbane next Sunday, a nation will be hoping history repeats itself.

New Zealand women maintained their 100% record of reaching the trophy match with a controlled 32-0 win over Samoa, spearheaded by a hat-trick for dual-code international Stacey Waaka.

But although yet to lose in the tournament, and having conceded just 24 points across four matches, New Zealand know they will face a stiff challenge from either three-time defending champions Australia or Fiji in the final.

"The tournament has been around building. How we started [an 18-12 win over Fiji] wasn't how we wanted to start – we got tested early, faced some adversity and challenges which will help us next week," said captain Georgia Hale.

"It's a challenge we are hungry for. The focus will be really internal, it's around our pack, our threat, what we can control, what we believe in. It will be a huge task but one we've been working towards for four years."

articles.title: New Zealand cruise to victory as Scotland fade at Murrayfield
articles.summary: New Zealand canter to a 43-21 Nations Championship win at Murrayfield as Scotland fall away after a thrilling first half.
articles.body:
Tries: Sititi, De Groot, Taylor, Barrett 2, Moorby, Aumua Cons: McKenzie 4

Ruthless New Zealand blew Scotland away in a high-class, seven tries to three Nations Championship victory at Murrayfield.

Despite a historic first-half hat-trick from Scotland hooker Ewan Ashman, the All Blacks were mostly magnificent, unrelenting and classy. It was the 34th Test between the nations and New Zealand's tally has yet another win - 32 now, with two draws going back to 1905.

Wallace Sititi scored early in a breathless first half. Ashman responded. Ethan de Groot and Codie Taylor hit back to make it 17-7 at the end of the first quarter.

New Zealand's Peter Lakai was binned and Ashman got his second while he was off. The sensational Beauden Barrett scored the first of his double straight after. Then, as the bonkerdom stretched on, Sititi was yellow-carded and Ashman made the All Blacks pay with his hat-trick try.

Only three points divided them at the break, but the All Blacks outclassed Scotland thereafter. Josh Moorby, Beauden Barrett again and Asafo Aumua struck in the second half. Scotland were beaten out the gate in the end.

We hoped for a classic and a classic it was, with bells on. If only for 40 minutes. Beyond that thrilling opening spell it was one-way traffic, a vicious exhibition of All Black class and might.

Just like last year, when New Zealand drew first blood, the visitors came roaring out, punishing a penalty given away cheaply with a piece of trickery at a close-range line-out that bamboozled the Scots. A couple of dummy runners broke away and took enough of Scotland's attention with them. Sititi thundered through a gap to score.

Thus began the ding-dong. Kyle Rowe's magnificent 50-22 gave Scotland the field position to strike off a driven line-out - Ashman driving over for the first of his three tries. Unlike his counterpart, Damian McKenzie, Finn Russell converted. Scotland led by two.

New Zealand turned the screw again, forcing Scotland into big defensive set after big defensive set. There's only so much of that you can soak up, though. The visitors looked lethal from all corners. Beauden Barrett's surge downfield, hotly pursued by Matt Fagerson, was the catalyst for their second score.

Fagerson was done on the floor, New Zealand went to touch and De Groot went over the line. McKenzie converted; New Zealand by five. And, soon, New Zealand by 10. Another Scotland penalty was punished to the max, the All Blacks executing from the resultant line-out maul. Taylor getting it down this time.

This all happened inside the first quarter. On it went. Lakai, the terrific openside, was binned for persistent New Zealand offsides. Huw Jones almost scored but got held up. Scotland came again. Off a penalty advantage, Ashman blasted through Sititi to score. Two for the hooker. With Russell's conversion it was a three-point game.

Scotland needed to kick on, but instead they got pushed back. The wondrous Beauden Barrett sliced through following huge work from his pack; on the face it simple, but in reality, complex and beautiful. McKenzie restored the 10-point lead, but it didn't last long.

Sititi was binned for going off his feet. Scotland had a crack at 13 All Blacks for a brief minute but couldn't break them despite going painfully close through Jones. Lakai returned to make it 15 versus 14 - and that's when Scotland struck.

It was that old reliable again, the line-out maul proving devastating. Ashman got on the end of it and over he went for his hat-trick. For a flurry of penalties and back-to-back yellows, New Zealand got what they deserved. Those cards cost them 14 points.

Seven first-half tries and three points between them at the break. Now it was time for Test match animals to emerge. When they did, they were wearing New Zealand white rather than Scotland blue.

The All Blacks played those key minutes in Scotland's 22, forcing errors and penalties and opportunities. Off a scrum, Jordie Barrett's skip pass found Moorby in space and he sauntered over. Ruthlessness again. McKenzie converted; 29-21. And worrying.

More New Zealand heat and more Scotland penalties. Then, a yellow for Sione Tuipulotu. It could have been Ben White just as easily. The pressure the visitors were applying was just suffocating.

With the captain off the pitch, New Zealand made it pay - Quinn Tupaea to McKenzie and on to Beauden Barrett for his second of the day. Skill-set through the roof.

McKenzie's conversion made it 36-21. At 50 minutes, the game was over far too early for Gregor Townsend's side. To rub salt in the wound Aumua finished a gorgeous set-piece to land try number seven; 43-21 and 19-0 in the second half.

Scotland had hopes of winning or, at the very least, of taking New Zealand to the wire. The uneasy truth for Townsend and his players is that despite their excellence in the opening half, they were utterly bossed in the second.

These All Blacks are far more formidable than the version that appeared at Murrayfield a year ago. Meanwhile, Scotland's long, long wait for glory against the Kiwis carries on and on.

Scotland: Kyle Rowe; Kyle Steyn, Huw Jones, Sione Tuipulotu (capt), Jamie Dobie; Finn Russell, Ben White; Rory Sutherland, Ewan Ashman, Zander Fagerson, Gregor Brown, Scott Cummings, Matt Fagerson, Rory Darge, Jack Dempsey.

Replacements: Gregor Hiddleston, Pierre Schoeman, Will Hurd, Max Williamson, Josh Baylish, George Horne, Tom Jordan, Blair Kinghorn.

New Zealand: Beauden Barrett; Will Jordan, Quinn Tupaea, Jordie Barrett, Josh Moorby; Damian McKenzie, Cam Roigard; Ethan de Groot, Codie Taylor (capt), Fletcher Newell, Scott Barrett, Fabian Holland, Tupou Vaa'i, Peter Lakai, Wallace Sititi.

Replacements: Asafo Aumua, George Bower, Pasilio Tosi, Christian Lio-Willie, Anton Segner, Cortez Ratima, Timoci Tavatavanawai, Rieko Ioane.

articles.title: Nations Championship schedule, results, kick-off times and how to watch
articles.summary: Everything you need to know as the inaugural edition of the competition continues
articles.body:
Rugby's Nations Championship bursts back into life as the inaugural edition comes to a conclusion in a busy November.

The new competition pits the Six Nations sides against the four Rugby Championship competitors, plus Japan and Fiji, across six matches split evenly across the July and November Test windows.

The results of those games will determine each of the 12 teams' seedings for the finals weekend at Twickenham's Allianz Stadium , with six matches contested over two days and both team and hemisphere silverware up for grabs.

Each entrant will be matched against the equivalent qualifier from the other pool to decide overall placings at the conclusion of a busy year of international action. France and South Africa currently top the two pools, with New Zealand also unbeaten and level on points with the Springboks.

Here's the full competition schedule, and how it will all work:

Announced during the 2023 Rugby World Cup, the new competition will be held every other year and replaces the traditional summer tours and Autumn Nations Series. It is designed to add context to the international calendar, with Fiji and Japan invited to join the Six Nations and Rugby Championship sides to form a top 12. Promotion and relegation is planned for the future with the second-tier Nations Cup, though will not take place in 2026.

Northern Hemisphere : France, Ireland, Scotland, Italy, England, Wales.

Southern Hemisphere: South Africa, New Zealand, Argentina, Australia, Fiji, Japan.

The first finals weekend will be held at Twickenham on the last weekend (27 to 29) of November. Three days of double-headers will be held at the ground, with the first-placed finisher of the Six Nations sides meeting whoever tops the other pool, and so on and so forth down the rankings.

The winner of that marquee match will lift the first Nations Championship trophy, while whichever hemisphere – a term used loosely with Japan included in the "southern" section and Fiji hosting their games in the United Kingdom – wins more final matches will also be crowned. The 1st vs 1st match is worth two points, with all other matches in the finals weekend worth one.

Viewers in the United Kingdom will be able to watch every game on ITV after the free-to-air broadcaster struck a deal to show the competition.
